# No Dig Beds

## Overview

The plot came with a weedy corner where the couch grass had been left to run for years. I read enough to know that turning that soil over with a spade would only chop the roots into pieces and give each piece a new start. Every cut root wakes a fresh plant, and the soil underneath loses the crumb structure that took the worms a decade to build. So I stopped digging the beds altogether and let the soil do the work. It is slower to look tidy and it is far less work in the back. The structure holds, the worms stay where they are, and I can plant into it the same season I cover it. This note is what I did in that corner and how it has gone since. The soil here is a heavy clay that sets like brick when it dries and holds water like a bucket when it rains. Digging it mostly made things worse: every spade went in and came out a smooth, smeared face, and the structure I broke down in spring was back to a pan by August. Left alone it has done better than it ever did under the fork, and the only tool I use on the beds themselves is a rake.

## Setup

The corner I had in mind was about eight metres by four, and it was solid couch grass from end to end. I stood on it in July with a fork in my hand, ready to dig it over the way I had done every other bed on the plot, and then I put the fork down. The roots were threaded through the top ten centimetres in a mat so dense that a spade would have cut thousands of viable pieces and I would have been weeding them out for three years. The choice was between a fortnight of hard digging followed by endless pulling, or covering the whole thing and waiting. I covered it.

The cover is plain brown cardboard, the sort that comes flattened behind the supermarket, laid straight onto the grass with every seam overlapped by 20 cm. I walked the seams so the flaps knitted down and no light could reach a join. Cardboard is the part that does the killing: it blocks the light, the grass exhausts itself under it, and in time it softens and rots into the soil where the worms drag it down. I laid it in a dry week so it did not turn to pulp under my boots. Where the cardboard met the grass at the edges I tucked the flaps under themselves rather than leaving a lip, because a lifted edge is exactly where the couch comes back.

On top of the cardboard went compost, about 10 cm of it across the whole area. That depth matters. Ten centimetres is enough for the roots of a lettuce or a beetroot to get hold, and it is the growing layer for the first season while the cardboard breaks down underneath. I barrowed it in and raked it level but did not tread it, and I did not mix it into the soil below. The whole point is that the layers stay layers: compost on top, rotted grass and cardboard in the middle, undisturbed soil at the base. A layer cake, not a pudding.

The paths took a little more thought. I set them 60 cm wide, which is wide enough for a barrow wheel and a boot without clipping the bed edges. Into those paths went woodchip, 5 cm of it, laid on a sheet of the same cardboard so the couch beneath would not push up through the chips. The broadfork came out only for the paths, not the beds. I push it in along the path line and lever it back to loosen the compacted strip, working backwards a step at a time, because a path that has been walked all winter sets like a board and water will not drain off it. The beds themselves have never seen the fork.

There is no edging anywhere. I looked at timber boards and at plastic strip and left both on the shelf. The raised timber edges I have used elsewhere give slugs somewhere to hide, dry the soil out at the rim, and cost money to replace when they rot. Here the compost just feathers into the woodchip and I rake the edges back into shape each time the surface needs tidying. It looks softer than a boxed bed and it takes me about ten minutes a season to keep the line where I want it.

The worms arrived without an invitation. By the October after I covered the corner I lifted a flap of cardboard at the edge and found a dozen of them in the damp mat underneath, pale and working the rot. By the following spring the count under a spade-sized square of the cover had gone from two or three to something like fifteen, and the cardboard had gone from stiff brown board to a soft grey rag you could tear with two fingers. That is the sign the thing is working: the cover is not a barrier any more, it is food.

The first autumn and winter were the quiet part. I planted nothing that year except a few winter salads into the compost layer in September, and left the rest to sit. The rain came through the compost and soaked the cardboard against the soil, and the frost lifted and dropped the surface a few times. By February the level had dropped by about 3 cm as the compost settled and the layers began to knit, so I raked the edges back up and filled the dip with a couple of barrows of spent potting mix. The couch under the cover had gone yellow, then white, then to nothing but threads.

Topping up is part of the job from the second year. Every autumn I add another 2 cm of compost across the surface and let the weather work it down. I do not dig it in and I do not turn the bed. The old layer feeds the new one from underneath, the worms carry the fresh material down through the profile, and the surface stays dark and loose without a fork ever touching it. It is the least dramatic gardening I do, and it is the corner of the plot that gives me the most.

## Maintenance

The whole upkeep is a barrow of compost once a year and a bit of tidying. In October I spread about 2 cm across each bed, straight onto whatever is left of the summer mulch, and let the worms pull it down through the winter. I do not fork it in and I do not turn the surface. Through the season I add a mulch of grass clippings or straw under the leafy crops once the soil has warmed, which keeps the moisture in and the weed seed from getting a start. I never walk on the beds. I keep to the woodchip paths and I reach across from the edge, and where a bed is too wide to reach I laid a stepping board down rather than tread the soil beside it. Clearing is the other half: I pull the old crop stems and leave the fine roots in the ground, cut the tops off the spent brassicas and lay them on the surface as a feed, and I do not clear the beds bare going into winter. A bare bed here caps into a crust by January and the rain runs off it instead of soaking in. I keep a rake by the bed for the small jobs and a bag of spent potting mix for patching.

## Planting

I plant in bands and keep the spacing generous, because crowded leaves sit damp and the slugs find them. Kale and chard go in at about 45 cm apart in a grid, which looks wide in May and looks right by August when each plant is a small bush. Spinach and leaf beet go in rows 25 cm apart with the plants thinned to 15 cm. Rocket and mustard I sow broadcast and cut young rather than spacing at all, since they are up and gone in a month. Succession is what keeps the kitchen supplied: I sow a short row of salad about every three weeks from March to September, and I follow a cleared row of early leaves with a sowing of the next crop straight away. When a band finishes I pull it, rake the surface level and sow the gap the same afternoon, so there is never a bare patch sitting long enough to grow weeds.

## Troubleshooting

Slugs are the main pest and they are worst in a wet spring. I lift any timber lying about, keep the paths mown short so there is no cover, and set the young plants out a little bigger than I would in a dug bed. The cardboard breaking down too fast is the other thing to watch. When I laid a thin single layer in one patch it rotted through in two months and the couch came up through the gaps, so now I always double it and overlap the seams well. Couch grass creeps back at the edges where the cover stops, and I cut it there with a hoe before it can send runners into the bed. If it gets a hold inside the bed I lift the plant it is climbing through and pull the white root out by hand.
